vacancy.title: AI Engineer
vacancy.summary: The City of Riverton is seeking an AI Engineer to build reliable, privacy-focused applications based on language models that assist residents and staff. The role involves taking these applications from prototype to production while ensuring explainability and quality.

requirements.text: A completed degree at bachelor level or higher in computer science, AI, data science or similar.
At least 3 years of experience with Python in production environments.
Demonstrable experience with applications based on language models (for example RAG).
Experience with CI/CD, containers (Docker) and version control (Git).
Design and build AI applications with language models (RAG, agents) in Python.
Take applications to production and run them, together with the platform team.
Measure answer quality and build guardrails against hallucinations.
Translate questions from policy and operations into feasible solutions and explain choices to non-technical colleagues.
Experience evaluating LLM output and building guardrails.
Knowledge of privacy law (GDPR) and working with personal data.
Experience with open-source or self-hosted language models.
Experience in the public sector or with complex stakeholders.

answers.topic: Open the interview and understand motivation for the role and organisation
answers.question: What draws you to this AI Engineer role at the City of Riverton, and how do you see yourself contributing to public-sector applications?
answers.answer:
What draws me most is that the AI directly helps residents. At Harbour Logistics I built an assistant for planners, and the best part wasn't the technology. It was seeing people do their work faster and with more confidence. At a city, that impact is even more direct: if a staff member can help a resident quickly and correctly, the resident feels it right away.

I also really like that reliability, privacy and explainability come first here, because that's already how I work. Every answer from our assistant has to cite its source, and no release goes live without passing our evaluation set. I'd bring exactly that discipline. My public-sector experience is limited to an internship at a water authority, so I'd lean on policy advisers for the context. The part where you make AI measurable and trustworthy, that I can bring from day one.

a_cv_consistency.rationale: The RAG assistant, evaluation set, and results described match the CV entries for Harbour Logistics.

a_overclaim.rationale: The claims about the assistant and evaluation set align with CV details without exaggeration.

a_req_resp_4.rationale: The answer discusses motivation and reliability practices but does not clearly demonstrate translating policy/operations questions into feasible solutions explained to non-technical colleagues.

strengths.text: You clearly connect your Harbour Logistics work to resident impact: 'it was seeing people do their work faster and with more confidence'
Good honesty about the limits of your public-sector experience, showing self-awareness

add.text: You didn't mention your GDPR/privacy work with a privacy officer at DataWorks, which is directly relevant to a public-sector employer's privacy concerns
Your meetup organising on open-source AI could show community engagement and communication skills relevant to explaining choices to non-technical stakeholders

Can you describe a time you explained a technical choice (like a guardrail or model limitation) to someone without a technical background?

outline.text: Open with motivation: AI that helps residents directly, echoing the planner assistant impact you saw at Harbour Logistics
Add your GDPR/privacy officer collaboration at DataWorks as evidence you already work within data protection constraints relevant to government work
Acknowledge your public-sector experience is limited to your water authority internship, and that you'd rely on policy advisers for context
Close by connecting your ability to explain technical choices clearly, as shown by organising your open-source AI meetup, to translating between technical and non-technical colleagues

answers.topic: Explore hands-on experience building and productionising LLM-based applications
answers.question: You mention taking applications to production with Docker and GitHub Actions on Kubernetes. Can you walk me through a specific instance where you handled versioning or CI/CD for an LLM-based application?
answers.answer:
Sure. The clearest example is how we release changes to the customs assistant at Harbour Logistics. Early on, a change to the prompt or the retrieval setup could quietly make answers worse, and we'd only find out when a planner complained. I wanted every change to be checked before it reached users.

So I set up a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds the Docker image and then runs our evaluation set of 200 verified questions against it. If the share of wrong answers goes up, the release is blocked. Only when the set passes does the image get deployed to the Kubernetes cluster. To be honest, my Kubernetes knowledge is fairly basic; the platform team runs the cluster, and I work with them on the deployment side.

The result: no release goes live without passing the set, and that's a big part of how we brought wrong answers down from 18% to 6%.

strengths.text: You gave a concrete, specific example: a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds the Docker image and gates deployment on an evaluation set of 200 questions before it reaches the Kubernetes cluster.
Nice honesty about acknowledging your Kubernetes knowledge is basic and that you collaborate with the platform team rather than overclaiming.

add.text: You didn't mention the guardrails you added (citations required, refuse when no source found) as part of the quality checks tied to this release process.
You didn't connect this to the concrete impact on planners, like the drop in average search time from 12 to 3 minutes.

explore.text: Do you have an example of how you decided what threshold or rollback strategy to use when the wrong-answer rate went up during a release?
Do you have an example of versioning specific components separately, like the prompt versus the retrieval index, so you could tell which change caused a regression?

outline.text: Set the problem: unchecked changes to prompts or retrieval could silently degrade answers for the customs assistant at Harbour Logistics.
Describe the pipeline: GitHub Actions builds the Docker image, then runs the 200-question evaluation set before deployment to Kubernetes.
Mention the guardrails (citations required, refuse when no source found) as another layer of quality control in the release process.
Be clear about ownership: you work with the platform team on Kubernetes since your knowledge there is more basic.
Close with impact: wrong answers dropped from 18% to 6%, and search time per question fell from 12 to 3 minutes.

answers.topic: Probe quality measurement, guardrails against hallucinations, and translating needs from non-technical stakeholders
answers.question: Tell me about a time you had to prove to non-technical stakeholders that an AI system's answers could be trusted, and how you approached measuring or improving that trust.
answers.answer: I think trust mostly comes from good communication. I always try to explain things clearly and involve stakeholders early, so they understand what the system does and what it doesn't do. I also try to be transparent about the limitations, because people trust you more when you're honest with them. And I make sure to keep them updated along the way, so there are no surprises at the end. In general, I've found that if you take people seriously and listen to their concerns, they're much more open to new technology.

strengths.text: You emphasized being transparent about limitations and involving stakeholders early, which is a good foundation for building trust

add.text: You didn't mention the evaluation set of 200 questions you built to measure answer quality and track improvement over iterations
You didn't mention the concrete guardrails you added—requiring citations and refusing to answer when no source is found—which directly address hallucination risk

You didn't mention your work with planners at Harbour Logistics, where the RAG assistant reduced search time from 12 to 3 minutes, which would be a strong concrete example for non-technical stakeholders

outline.text: Start with a concrete case: built a RAG assistant for planners answering customs questions, used by many stakeholders
Explain how you measured quality with an evaluation set of 200 verified questions, showing wrong answers dropped from 18% to 6% over three iterations
Describe the guardrails you introduced—mandatory citations and refusal when no source is found—to prevent hallucinations

answers.topic: Probe quality measurement, guardrails against hallucinations, and translating needs from non-technical stakeholders
answers.question: You mentioned communicating with non-technical stakeholders to build trust, but your response focused on general principles rather than a specific instance. Can you describe a concrete situation where you had to explain a limitation of an AI system to a skeptical policy adviser and what the outcome was?
answers.answer:
Sure. I haven't worked with policy advisers yet, but the closest situation was at Harbour Logistics, when I demoed the customs assistant to the management team. One of them was quite skeptical. During the demo the assistant answered one question with "I don't know," and he asked why we'd roll out something that can't answer everything.

I explained in plain words that this was deliberate. The assistant only answers when it can find the rule in our documents, and it always shows the source. If it can't find one, it says so, because a confident wrong answer on customs rules costs far more than a planner spending a few minutes checking. I backed that up with our evaluation results: wrong answers had come down from 18% to 6%, largely because of that refusal behaviour.

After that he was on board, and the "I don't know" behaviour stayed in as a feature.

a_req_wens_4.rationale: The example involves a management team at a company, not a public sector context or policy adviser, and the candidate explicitly states they haven't worked with policy advisers.

strengths.text: Good use of a concrete example instead of general principles: the skeptical manager, the 'I don't know' moment, and the outcome that it stayed as a feature.
You backed up your explanation with a clear metric (wrong answers down from 18% to 6%), which is convincing evidence for a skeptical audience.

add.text: You didn't mention the citation requirement guardrail explicitly, which is part of what convinced the manager the system was trustworthy.
You didn't mention your experience working with a privacy officer under GDPR, which is another example of translating technical/compliance constraints for a non-technical stakeholder.

explore.text: Do you have an example where you explained an AI limitation specifically to someone in a policy or government role, rather than a management team, since the question asked about a policy adviser?
Was there any resistance or follow-up questions from the manager after you showed the evaluation numbers, and how did you handle pushback in the moment?

outline.text: Set the scene: skeptical manager during the customs assistant demo questioned why it said 'I don't know'.
Explain the guardrail design: answers only given with a source citation, refusal when no rule is found.
Give the reasoning: a wrong customs answer costs more than a planner double-checking.
Support with data: error rate dropped from 18% to 6% over iterations, largely due to refusal behavior.
Outcome: manager was convinced, and the refusal behavior stayed as a permanent feature.

answers.topic: Close the interview and invite candidate questions
answers.question: That covers what I wanted to ask — what questions do you have for us about the role or the team?
answers.answer:
Thanks, I have two.

First: how do you decide when an AI application is good enough to put in front of residents? I'm curious whether you already have fixed criteria for that, or whether it's weighed per application.

And second: who in the team owns the evaluation of model output once something is live? In my experience, that's the moment quality can quietly slip if nobody is clearly responsible for it.

a_quality.rationale: The candidate asks thoughtful, relevant questions but this is a candidate-question exchange, not a structured example with result and reflection, so it doesn't fit a STAR-style answer.

a_star_s.rationale: This is a closing Q&A response, not a situation description as expected in a STAR-format behavioral answer.

a_star_a.rationale: The response consists of questions to the interviewer, not a description of actions the candidate took.

add.text: You could have grounded your second question in your own experience of setting up an evaluation set and tracking wrong-answer rates over iterations, which would show this isn't just a theoretical concern for you.

explore.text: Do you have a concrete example of a time when evaluation ownership was unclear on one of your projects and quality started to slip, which you could reference if asked to elaborate on your second question?

outline.text: Ask how they decide when an AI application is ready for residents — fixed criteria or case-by-case.
Ask who owns ongoing evaluation of model output once live, noting that in your experience this is where quality can slip without clear ownership.
Tie it back to your guardrails work (citations required, refuse when no source found) as an example of building in accountability from the start.
